title: Multimodal fusion strategies in 2026: token concat, cross-attention, Q-Former
summary: An empirical comparison of how modern VLMs combine modalities. Token concat dominates open-source; cross-attention re-emerges for long-context; Q-Former / resamplers are the middle ground. Where each wins and the design space for 2026.
abstract: Three years after CLIP and Flamingo established multimodal fusion as a research area, the architectural landscape has narrowed but not converged. Open-source VLMs (LLaVA, Qwen-VL, InternVL, Idefics) have largely settled on token concatenation: project image features to LLM token embedding space, concatenate with text tokens, feed into the LLM's standard self-attention. Cross-attention (Flamingo, BLIP-2) re-emerges for long-context, frozen-LLM, and streaming scenarios. Q-Former and resampler architectures occupy a useful middle ground when fixed image-token counts matter. This paper surveys the 2026 state, the empirical trade-offs, and recommendations for picking a fusion strategy by use case.
contentIntro:
## What's compared

Three fusion strategies dominate modern VLMs:

- **Token concatenation** (LLaVA-style): unified self-attention over image and text tokens. Simple; the open-source default.
- **Cross-attention** (Flamingo, BLIP-2): text stream + dedicated cross-attention to image features. Cleaner long-context handling.
- **Q-Former / resampler** (BLIP-2, Qwen-VL): compress many image patches to a fixed number of query tokens before fusing.

This paper covers when each is the right choice and where the ecosystem is heading.

contentUndergrad:
## The empirical state

**Token concatenation** dominates open-source. LLaVA, Qwen-VL, InternVL, Idefics, Pixtral — all use some flavor of token concat.

```
image → vision_encoder → image_features
image_features → projection → image_tokens (LLM token embedding space)
[image_tokens, text_tokens] → LLM → response
```

Reasons:
- Implementation simplicity. Bolt a vision encoder onto an LLM with minimal architectural changes.
- Reuses LLM's pretrained self-attention apparatus.
- Empirically matches Flamingo-style cross-attention at the parameter scales open-source operates.

**Cross-attention** (Flamingo, BLIP-2 cross-attn variant): the LLM's main token stream stays text-only; cross-attention layers attend to image features.

```
for each layer:
    self_attention(text_tokens)
    cross_attention(text_tokens, image_features)
    FFN(text_tokens)
```

Reasons it survives:
- Long-context multimodal: image features stay separate; don't consume context.
- Frozen-LLM scenarios: add cross-attention layers without modifying the LLM.
- Streaming: image features computed once; reused across multiple text generations.

**Q-Former / resampler** (BLIP-2, Qwen-VL): a small transformer compresses 256-1024 patch features into a fixed (e.g., 32-64) number of query tokens.

```
image_features → Q-Former → fixed-count query tokens
query tokens → LLM (concat with text or cross-attention)
```

Reasons:
- Fixed token count for variable-resolution images.
- Compression: large feature maps don't bloat context.
- Composable: works with either token concat or cross-attention downstream.

## Empirical comparison

Apples-to-apples comparisons are rare (different recipes, different data). The published results that exist:

| Architecture | Backbone | MMMU | MM-Vet | DocVQA | Latency |
|--------------|----------|------|--------|--------|---------|
| LLaVA-1.5 (concat) | Llama-2 7B | 35 | 31 | 28 | 1.0× ref |
| BLIP-2 (Q-Former + cross-attn) | Vicuna 13B | 30 | 27 | 31 | 1.1× |
| Idefics2 (concat) | Mistral 7B | 39 | 36 | 67 | 1.0× |
| Flamingo-9B (cross-attn) | Chinchilla 7B | -- | -- | -- | 0.9× |

(Gaps reflect benchmarks not all models report on.)

Key observations:
- Token concat (LLaVA, Idefics2) and cross-attention (Flamingo) are within ~5 points on most benchmarks at similar parameter counts.
- Q-Former + cross-attention (BLIP-2) lags slightly; the compression is lossy at this scale.
- Latency differences are small (<10%); architectural choice isn't latency-driven.

The practical takeaway: pick based on your specific constraints, not on architectural quality differences.
contentGrad:
## When each wins

### Token concatenation

**Wins for**:
- Standard VQA / chat / instruction-following.
- Single-image inputs at standard resolution (224×224 to 1024×1024).
- Open-source projects where simplicity matters.
- Teams that want to leverage the LLM's full reasoning capacity.

**Loses for**:
- Long-context multimodal (many images, video).
- Frozen-LLM scenarios.

### Cross-attention

**Wins for**:
- Long-context: multiple images interleaved with text. Image features stay out of the token stream.
- Frozen-LLM: add capability without modifying the LLM.
- Streaming: image features cached and reused.
- Frontier-scale where the engineering complexity is justified.

**Loses for**:
- Open-source where simplicity wins.
- Settings where the LLM should be heavily fine-tuned for the multimodal task.

### Q-Former / resampler

**Wins for**:
- Variable-resolution images: fixed token count regardless of input size.
- Cases where the LLM context budget is tight.
- Multi-image inputs where you need to bound total token consumption.

**Loses for**:
- Standard single-image at standard resolution: the compression doesn't pay off.
- Tasks needing fine-grained spatial features: Q-Former smooths over them.

## Hybrid pipelines in production

Real multimodal apps typically use **hybrid** approaches:

- **Retrieval**: CLIP-style late fusion for image search at scale (precompute embeddings; index in Faiss).
- **Reasoning**: token-concat VLM for detailed analysis of retrieved images.
- **Long-context**: cross-attention or Q-Former for documents with many pages.

Common production stack:

```
user query → CLIP retrieval → top-K images
           → token-concat VLM (LLaVA-1.5+ or commercial GPT-4V)
           → response
```

This is what enterprise document AI, image search, and most multimodal copilots actually do. Pure architectures don't scale to the diverse requirements.

## Where the field is going

Three active fronts:

**1. Native multimodal at training time**. GPT-4o, Gemini Ultra are trained from scratch as multimodal — not as text LLMs with vision bolted on. Image, audio, text all in one transformer from day 1. Token-concat-style but with discrete tokens for non-text modalities.

**2. Video and long-context multimodal**. 60-minute video at 1 fps = 3600 frames; even with aggressive token reduction, this strains context. Cross-attention re-emerges as a serious option here. Streaming architectures (compute features once; access via cross-attention as text generates).

**3. Mixture-of-experts for multimodal**. Different experts handle different modalities; the router learns which expert to use for each token. Early results (DeepSeek-VL2, some Gemini variants) suggest the MoE pattern works for multimodal as well as for text-only.

## Recommendation matrix

For a team building a multimodal system in 2026:

**Standard chat / VQA / single-image instruction**: token concat (LLaVA-style). Use LLaVA-1.6 or Qwen2-VL as a starting point.

**Document AI / multi-page**: Q-Former for fixed token count + token concat downstream. Idefics2-style.

**Image retrieval at scale**: late fusion (CLIP). OpenCLIP ViT-L/14 or ViT-bigG.

**Long video**: cross-attention or sliding-window approaches. Niche; expect rapid evolution.

**Frontier-scale (GPT-4V class)**: native multimodal training. Out of reach for most teams; for now, leverage closed-source via APIs.

The architectural landscape is narrower than it was three years ago but not converged. Pick by use case; don't chase a single 'right answer'.
